name: Access Control Models
intent: Decide who may do what to which object, and pick a model (ACL, RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC) whose rules you can still reason about when the product has teams, folders and per-document sharing.
scenario: A shared documents app. Alice leads the eng team and bob is a member. Folders hold documents, a folder inherits from its parent, one document is shared with a contractor (dave), and alice keeps a private note. When bob opens eng/plan, the API asks an authorization service whether bob may view it.
problem: Authentication says who is calling. Authorization has to answer a different question on every request: may this subject perform this action on this object? The answer depends on teams, folders, ownership, sharing links and context, and it changes whenever someone joins a team or a file moves. Hard-coded if-statements spread through the codebase, rules nobody can audit, roles that multiply until nobody knows what they grant, and one over-broad rule that exposes everything are how this goes wrong.

howItWorks.title: Name the question: subject, action, resource, context
howItWorks.text: Every model answers check(subject, action, resource, context) with allow or deny. Start deny by default: access exists only if some rule grants it, so a missing rule fails safe. Grant the least that does the job, and keep authentication (proving who you are, covered in authentication-and-authorization) as a separate step that only supplies the subject.

howItWorks.title: ACL and RBAC: lists and roles
howItWorks.text: An ACL stores entries on each object (user:dave view). It answers 'who can open this file' in one read, but it grows with the number of objects and a new document starts empty. RBAC gives users roles and roles permissions, so onboarding is one assignment. It breaks down when permissions are per resource: one role per team and level gives 2 roles per team, which is role explosion, while a few coarse roles over-grant. Separation of duties is a role rule: no one may hold both 'requester' and 'approver', or approve their own request.

howItWorks.title: ABAC: rules over attributes
howItWorks.text: Attribute-based control evaluates a rule over attributes of the user, the resource and the context: allow view if user.team == doc.team and the request is in business hours. Four rules can cover a thousand teams and nothing changes when a team is added. The price is auditability. 'Who can view this document?' has no stored answer: you must evaluate the rules for every user, and one wrong OR exposes everything.

howItWorks.title: ReBAC: relationships and graph traversal
howItWorks.text: Google Zanzibar (2019) stores relation tuples such as doc:readme#viewer@user:alice, group:eng#member@user:bob and folder:eng#viewer@group:eng#member. A schema of userset rewrites says viewer includes editor, and a document's viewers include its parent folder's viewers. check() walks these tuples as a graph with a depth bound: document, parent folder, group, user. This is how Drive and GitHub sharing behave, and open-source servers (SpiceDB, OpenFGA, Ory Keto) copy it. Sharing a folder is one tuple that every file under it inherits.

howItWorks.title: Policy engines and policy as code
howItWorks.text: Open Policy Agent (Rego) and AWS Cedar move rules out of application code into a policy language evaluated by a decision point, with the application as the enforcement point. Policies live in git, get reviewed, tested and rolled out like code. Cedar is default deny, an explicit forbid beats any permit, and its analysis can prove properties such as 'no policy makes a document public'. OPA does not store your relationships: you feed it the data (attributes, tuples) it decides over.

howItWorks.title: Enforce on every request, close the confused deputy, expect lag
howItWorks.text: Enforce where the object is known: a gateway can check coarse things (is this token valid, does it carry the scope), but only the service holding the document id can do the resource check, and it must do it for every request, including internal calls. A service that acts with its own broad rights for a caller is a confused deputy (Norm Hardy, 1988): make it check the original caller, not its own authority. Caching decisions for 5 to 60 seconds saves traffic but every cached allow is also a revocation lag of that length, so decide how stale a removed user may remain.

pros: Deny by default plus least privilege means a forgotten rule fails closed, not open
RBAC is easy to explain, easy to assign at scale, and maps to how companies talk about jobs
ABAC needs no per-object upkeep: a constant number of rules covers any number of objects
ReBAC models sharing, nesting and inheritance directly and can answer both 'can X?' and 'who can?'
Policy as code makes access rules reviewable, testable and versioned
cons: ACLs grow with every object and drift: a new file does not inherit the sharing of its folder
RBAC either explodes in roles (per team, per level, per exception) or over-grants with a few coarse ones
ABAC is flexible but hard to audit: you cannot list who has access without evaluating every user
ReBAC needs a relationship store, a schema and tuple writes kept in step with your application data
A central decision service adds a hop on every request and becomes a critical dependency
whenToUse: ACL: a small number of objects with explicit sharing, such as file permissions or a storage bucket policy
RBAC: internal tools and admin consoles where permissions follow job function and do not vary by object
ABAC: rules that are naturally about attributes and context (same department, region, time, data classification)
ReBAC: user-facing sharing with groups, folders, teams and inheritance, where the question is 'how are these two related'
A policy engine once the same rules must be enforced consistently across several services
whenNotToUse: Do not run a Zanzibar-style relationship store for an app with three fixed roles: a column and an if-statement is easier to get right
Do not use RBAC alone for per-document sharing; the roles will outnumber the people
Do not use ABAC where auditors need a standing answer to 'who can see this', unless you can enumerate by evaluation
Do not centralize decisions if every check would add a network hop you cannot afford and the rules are trivial and local
Do not treat any of these as a substitute for authentication, input validation or encryption
pitfalls: Checking only at the gateway or the UI: the service behind it is then open to anyone who reaches it, and object-level authorization failures (BOLA, OWASP API Security number 1) are the most common API vulnerability
A confused deputy: a backend job or integration that reads any file with its own service account on behalf of whoever asked, so a low-privilege caller reaches high-privilege data
Roles baked into long-lived tokens: removing someone from a role does nothing until the token expires, often 5 to 60 minutes
Caching allow decisions without a TTL or a revision: a removed user keeps access, and the 'new enemy' problem appears when an old permission snapshot is paired with new content
Tests that only cover the allowed cases: the bugs are in the denied ones, so assert denies, including every user and resource pair on a small model
Unbounded graph walks and group cycles: always bound the depth and decide that hitting the limit means deny
Deny rules sprinkled on top of allow rules without a clear precedence, so no one can predict the outcome; pick one rule (explicit deny wins, as in Cedar and AWS IAM) and keep it

roles.label: Subject
roles.description: The authenticated user or service making the request.

roles.label: Enforcement point
roles.description: The API that asks 'may they?' before touching the document, on every request.

roles.label: Decision point
roles.description: The authorization service or policy engine that evaluates the rules and returns allow or deny.

roles.label: Relationship store
roles.description: Holds the facts the decision uses: tuples, roles, attributes.

roles.label: Decision cache
roles.description: Remembers recent answers for a short time to save calls, at the cost of revocation lag.

quiz.question: A photo-sharing app lets users share any album with friends, family groups and single people, and shared albums can sit inside shared folders. The team started with RBAC and now has 4,000 roles such as album_8812_viewer. What is the best fix?
options: Collapse everything into coarse viewer and editor roles granted across the whole app
Keep RBAC but generate the per-album roles automatically so admins stop creating them
Switch to ReBAC, so sharing is a stored relation that child objects inherit
Copy each album's sharing list onto every photo inside it as ACL entries
quiz.explanation: The permissions depend on how users, groups and objects relate, which is what ReBAC stores and walks. Coarse roles would over-grant, and per-photo ACLs drift when an album's sharing changes.

quiz.question: A document service lets editors read a file only if user.department equals doc.department. An auditor now asks for a list of everyone who can read the Q3 salary file. The service uses ABAC rules only, with no stored grants. What is the real difficulty?
options: Nothing stores the answer, so every user must be evaluated against that one file
The rules cannot express a department match unless extra roles are added first
ABAC checks run only at the gateway, where the file itself is not visible
Attribute rules deny everything by default, so the answer is simply an empty list
quiz.explanation: ABAC computes decisions on demand from attributes, so there is nothing to look up for 'who can'. The rules can express the match fine, and default deny does not empty the list.

quiz.question: A report service runs a nightly export job with its own service account that can read every tenant's files. The API lets any logged-in user request 'export file X' and the job reads X and emails it. Tenant A's user asks for tenant B's file and receives it. What is the best fix?
options: Add a gateway rule that blocks all export requests that come from tenant A users
Shorten the job's service account token lifetime so it expires within five minutes
Hide the export button in the UI for every file the user is not allowed to see
Make the job check the original requester's rights on the file before it reads the file
quiz.explanation: The job is a confused deputy: it uses its own broad rights for a caller. It must authorise the original caller on that object. Gateway rules, short tokens and UI hiding do not check the object.
